sentences.text: We will use binary search to find a target in a sorted array.
At each step, compare the target with the middle element.
The comparison lets us discard one half of the remaining array.
A useful way to think about that comparison is as receiving one bit of information.
It answers a yes-or-no question about which half can still contain the target.
That information view is why repeatedly halving a search space leads to a logarithm.
Remember the invariant from earlier: if the target exists, it remains inside the active interval.
Every boundary update must preserve that statement before the next comparison.
This connects the pseudocode to the loop-invariant proof rather than treating them as separate topics.
I first learned binary search by looking up names in my grandparents' phone directory.
That directory had a bright red cover and was extremely heavy.
The color of the book has no bearing on the algorithm.
In practice, choose one interval convention before writing any boundary updates.
I prefer a half-open interval because its size is always right minus left.
Most off-by-one bugs come from silently mixing closed and half-open conventions.
